tldr: We introduce Video2World, a benchmark that tests whether coding agents can autonomously build interactive physics simulation environments and robot behaviors from real-world and human demonstration videos. While frontier models can write code that runs in a simulator, their full task success rate remains around 15% to 37%, revealing that visual geometric fidelity does not always align with task success.
hero_caption: An overview of Video2World. A coding agent builds an interactive simulator from real-world RGB videos, evaluated along three axes: geometric fidelity, dynamic fidelity, and functional correctness (task success). It also highlights a sharp rise in task success rates with the emergence of frontier models.
overview:
Collecting data to train robots in the real world is expensive, making simulator-based Real-to-Sim techniques a hot topic. However, traditional approaches require heavy manual labor for placing 3D assets, tuning physical parameters, and calibrating coordinate frames.

To address this, the authors leveraged frontier foundation models and coding agents, framing the challenge as a software engineering task: taking a video as input, automatically generating both environment construction code and robot control code end to end, and interactively debugging them. To properly benchmark this capability, they created Video2World, a new benchmark featuring 222 evaluation instances derived from 189 human and robot demonstration videos.

In the experiments, they evaluated 9 frontier coding-agent systems on a shared interface. The evaluation spans three axes: Geometric Fidelity for initial configurations, Dynamic Fidelity for tracking object trajectories, and Functional Correctness for determining whether the task is physically completed through interaction.

The results show that while the latest models (such as Claude Fable 5.1) reliably produce executable code that spins up in a simulator, complete task success reaches only around 37%. Furthermore, models with more accurate visual geometries do not always succeed at tasks, highlighting that the gap between perceptual realism and factual correctness in generative models is also prominent in physical simulation.
contributions: Formulated the end-to-end autonomous construction of interactive simulators and robot behaviors from video as a software engineering task with execution feedback.
Built Video2World, a large-scale benchmark comprising 39 task families and 222 evaluation instances derived from 189 human and robot manipulation videos.
Designed an evaluation protocol that disentangles simulator reconstruction along three orthogonal axes: Geometric Fidelity, Dynamic Fidelity, and Functional Correctness (task success).
Evaluated 9 frontier coding agents under a unified standard, revealing a sharp performance surge across model generations as well as a disconnect between visual appeal and task executability.

sections.heading: Can You Build a Playable Simulator Just by Showing a Video?
sections.summary: To gather diverse real-world interaction data, there is a growing demand to generate entire physics simulators directly from videos. This paper treats this challenge as an autonomous software engineering task for coding agents and introduces Video2World to evaluate it comprehensively.
sections.details:
Robots need massive amounts of interaction data to operate dexterously in the physical world, but real-world data collection is time-consuming and expensive. Using simulators as data generation engines is a popular alternative. However, conventional Real-to-Sim techniques (replicating real-world phenomena in a simulator) require substantial human engineering effort to place 3D models and calibrate friction and mass.

Recent foundation models and coding agents have rapidly advanced in spatial perception, reasoning, and code generation. If an agent could watch a video, automatically write environment definition code and robot action scripts, and fix errors using execution logs, this data creation pipeline could be automated end to end.

Yet, existing benchmarks only measure isolated capabilities, such as 3D shape reconstruction or intuitive physics understanding. This work introduces Video2World, a comprehensive benchmark where agents write code for environments and robot control end to end from video and refine it with execution feedback. It rigorously tests agent abilities across three axes: shape accuracy (geometry), object motion reproduction (dynamics), and physical task completion (functionality).

sections.heading: Building Simulators from Video: Problem Formulation
sections.summary: The video-to-sim task is formulated as a program synthesis problem that generates both simulator environment definitions and robot control code from video. The agent refines its code through trial and error in a sandbox environment.
sections.details:
This study frames the video-to-simulation task as synthesizing an executable program $P = (\eta, \pi)$. Here, $\eta$ represents environment specifications such as object geometries, initial poses, collision models, and mass, while $\pi$ denotes robot action specifications matched to the simulator's interface.

Executing this program generates rollouts of state transitions $s_{t+1} = F_\eta(s_t, a_t)$ driven by environment dynamics $F_\eta$ and robot actions $a_t$. A program is deemed functionally correct when the simulated robot successfully reproduces the task depicted in the video.

The agent's workflow is fully iterative coding. The agent receives an RGB video $v$, simulator APIs, and general coding tools. It writes code, runs the simulator locally, inspects rendered images and execution logs, and fixes discrepancies. Once time budgets or tool call limits are reached, or when the agent declares completion, the final submitted code is frozen and evaluated.

sections.heading: Designing Video2World and Its Three Evaluation Axes
sections.summary: The benchmark provides 222 evaluation instances spanning robot and human demonstration videos. It objectively evaluates agents independently of their internal implementation across build rate, geometric fidelity, dynamic fidelity, and functional correctness.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Benchmark Construction
The evaluation dataset curates 189 video clips (222 instances across 39 task families) from FurnitureBench, DROID, RoboDojo, HOI4D, HOT3D, DexYCB, OakInk2, and custom real-world home environments. It includes robot hand videos as well as first-person and third-person human hand manipulation videos. Each instance is annotated with 3D object geometries and initial poses (geometry), temporal object trajectories (kinematics), and preconditions, event sequences, and final goals needed for task success (specifications). For human videos, hand trajectories are pre-verified to ensure they are physically feasible when mapped to a robot end-effector.

### 3.2 Agent Protocol Design
Agents operate within an isolated sandbox environment. They are provided with video files, API documentation, 3D assets, and standard shell tools, allowing them to autonomously debug code while running simulations locally. However, access to ground-truth 3D meshes, trajectory data, and hidden evaluation scripts is strictly blocked.

### 3.3 Metric Design
Reconstructed worlds are strictly scored along the following dimensions:
- **Build Rate (Executability)**: The percentage of submitted code that initializes and steps through the simulator without errors.
- **Geometric Fidelity**: Measures object shapes, sizes, initial poses, and overall scene consistency using metrics like Chamfer Distance on point clouds. Higher weights are assigned to task-relevant objects such as manipulated items and receptacles.
- **Dynamic Fidelity**: Evaluates how well simulated translational and rotational object trajectories match real object motion in the video using Absolute Pose Error (APE) and Relative Pose Error (RPE).
- **Functional Correctness**: The most critical dimension, evaluating whether the robot successfully completes the task in physical simulation (Task Success) and how many intermediate milestones it reaches (Task Progress).

sections.heading: Frontier Agent Capabilities and the "Look vs. Function" Gap
sections.summary: Evaluating 9 frontier coding agents reveals a sharp improvement in task success with models like Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. However, reconstructing clean 3D object shapes and physically completing a task turn out to be two very different challenges.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The experiment compares 9 systems: Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3, Qwen 3.8-Max, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and GLM-5.3 Flash. Each agent is given up to 180 minutes of execution time per instance. In addition, a Human-Assisted Reference (HAR), manually tuned by humans with access to ground-truth information, serves as an estimated upper bound.

### 4.2 Key Results
- **Executable but Hard to Complete**: Most agents achieve a high Build Rate, successfully spinning up error-free simulation environments. However, Task Success (fully completing the task) remained below 5% for models prior to Claude Opus 5, and reached 37.67% even with the latest Claude Fable 5.1. Task Progress, which tracks intermediate milestones, is consistently higher, highlighting that agents often execute initial stages but struggle to complete tasks through to the end.
- **The Look vs. Function Gap**: GPT-6 Astra ranked top in geometric accuracy for object shapes and sizes, yet Claude Fable 5.1 outperformed it in task success. In short, looking just like the original video does not guarantee that the robot can grasp and manipulate objects properly. Conversely, in some cases, robot action trajectories adapted well enough to succeed even when initial poses or geometries had slight errors.
- **Even Human References Fall Short**: Even HAR, tuned by humans consulting annotations, achieved only a 58.8% task success rate. This illustrates how difficult it is to reproduce contact-rich physical dynamics.
- **Kinematic Fidelity of End-Effector Motion**: In successful simulation runs, robot end-effector statistics (travel distance, peak velocity, rotation magnitude, etc.) showed strong Spearman correlation (0.74 to 0.99) with the original videos, confirming that dynamics along the way are faithfully reproduced, not just final outcomes.

captions.F5: Comparison of robot end-effector kinematic statistics (duration, travel distance, max velocity, lift height, etc.) between real videos and simulator reproductions. Successful runs exhibit strong correlations (coefficients 0.74 to 0.99).

sections.heading: Distinct from Prior Work: Moving from Partial 3D Reconstruction to Integrated World Modeling
sections.summary: This section reviews prior Real-to-Sim research, LLM agents for robotics, and coding benchmarks, highlighting the unique nature of this benchmark in tackling both environment construction and action control end to end with execution feedback.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of three main research areas.

The first is Real-to-Sim techniques for robot manipulation. Studies like RialTo and Re3Sim reconstruct environments for policy learning, while works like GenSim and Video2Policy leverage foundation models to generate tasks or rewards. However, these rely on specialized pipelines and stop short of fully automated end-to-end construction and verification from video.

The second is foundation model agents for embodied tasks. Frameworks like Code as Policies and VoxPoser drive robots via code, and systems like Voyager acquire skills using execution feedback. This study takes that idea further: agents write not only robot control code, but the entire physical simulation environment itself as executable code.

The third is coding and generation benchmarks. While benchmarks like SWE-bench evaluate software engineering, 3DCodeBench tests 3D procedural generation, and BVB evaluates Blender scene reconstruction, none directly test whether a robot can physically interact and complete tasks by integrating physics engines with action control.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: The authors introduced Video2World, a benchmark for autonomously constructing interactive simulations from video. They conclude on the difficulty of building worlds that physically work beyond visual geometric fidelity, underscoring the necessity of integrated evaluation.
sections.details:
This paper proposed Video2World, a new benchmark evaluating the ability to autonomously construct interactive physics simulation environments from embodied videos. By formulating video-to-simulation generation and debugging as a software engineering task, it provides a comprehensive assessment across geometry, dynamics, and functional correctness.

Experimental findings reveal that while frontier coding agents can now write syntactically valid code that runs in simulators, fully completing tasks with physical interaction remains a major hurdle. In particular, the discovery that a visually accurate world does not necessarily equal a physically functional world strongly suggests that future research on world models and video-based data generation must adopt execution-based evaluation beyond mere pixel matching.

sections.heading: Appendix: Detailed Evaluation Specs and Case Studies
sections.summary: An explanation of the agent input/output interfaces, rigorous per-object task success criteria, and concrete failure and success case studies supporting the "look vs. function" disconnect.
sections.details:
### Interface and Sandbox Environment
Agents receive video files, camera specifications, target robot URDFs, and simulator API documentation. The simulation backends use SAPIEN (rigid-body manipulation), MuJoCo (deformable objects like ropes and plushies), and Isaac Sim (real-world home tasks). The robot control interfaces are specified per task, such as single-arm Cartesian TCP control (position, quaternion, gripper state), 5-finger Wuji hand joint angle control, or dual-arm joint angle control.

### Strict Task Success Criteria
Each task family features strict, physics-grounded evaluation criteria. For example, in the "unplug pen from holder" task, at least 95% of the pen's vertices must come to rest outside the holder's horizontal footprint (if the robot pulls the pen up but it remains inside the container, it counts as a failure). In the "bottle uprighting" task, the bottle's major axis must remain within 30 degrees of the table surface normal and rest supported by the table.

### Case Studies: Look vs. Function Disconnect
As shown in Figures F8 and F9, even when generated object sizes or shapes deviate by several centimeters from the original video, or when rotation angles diverge significantly, tasks like block stacking or bottle uprighting can succeed if the robot's trajectory aligns with that placement. Conversely, even with high-accuracy 3D mesh reconstruction, tasks fail if the gripper does not pull up far enough and leaves the pen in the container. These concrete examples confirm that geometric error and task success must be evaluated independently.

captions.F7: GPT-6 Astra execution on the DROID bottle uprighting task. Despite temporal and geometric deviations in object trajectory and height (average APE of 7.77 cm) compared to the original video, it successfully clears the criteria for uprighting and stabilizing the bottle.
captions.F8: Examples illustrating the disconnect between geometric fidelity and task success. In (a), the marker does not fully exit the container despite robot motion, resulting in failure; in (b), the bottle uprighting task succeeds despite large errors in shape and size.
captions.F9: An example where a task succeeds despite large errors in object pose (rotation angle). Although the block has a large absolute orientation error, the relative grasp-and-place relationship in simulation is consistent, leading to successful block stacking.

takeaways: In Video-to-Sim, where simulators and control programs are written simultaneously from video, frontier agents can now reliably output running code.
Task success rates surged after Claude Opus 5 (jumping from under 5% to over 37%), yet still lag behind human-assisted tuning (around 59%).
Accurate 3D visual geometry does not guarantee successful physical interaction; simulator utility cannot be judged by visual generative quality alone.
Automating simulator-based data scaling requires agent capabilities that can debug contact physics and robot control alignment simultaneously, not just scene appearance.
limitations: Even the Human-Assisted Reference (HAR), tuned with ground-truth annotations, achieves only around 59% success, indicating that the sensitivity of contact physics simulation itself caps the score ceiling.
Agents are allocated generous resources (up to 180 minutes and $60 in API costs per instance), making real-time, on-site reconstruction still cost-prohibitive.
Task success evaluation relies on geometric state transitions (relative positions and contact states), which does not fully capture the fidelity of contact forces or fastening torques.
